Source text (read all of it):
<<<
Backyard Barbecue: Smoker and Grill

Two cooks, one offset smoker, one kettle grill, one side burner and a cooler for holding. The pork owns the smoker all day; everything else happens in the last two hours.

Pork shoulder
Light the smoker and bring it to 250°F; 45 minutes. While it comes up, trim the shoulder and rub it heavily with salt, pepper and paprika; 25 minutes. Put the shoulder on once the smoker holds temperature and smoke it unwrapped for 6 hours, until the bark is dark and set. Wrap it tightly in butcher paper; 10 minutes. Back on the smoker, wrapped, until the thickest part probes soft — usually another 3 hours, sometimes four. Hold it wrapped in a cooler for one to three hours; it will not get cold and it only gets better. Pull the meat by hand; 30 minutes.

Beans
When the pork goes into the cooler, fry the bacon and onion in the pot on the side burner for 12 minutes, then add the beans, molasses and a ladle of drippings and let them tick over on the lowest flame until you serve.

Slaw
Start the slaw at the same time. Shred the cabbage and carrot; 20 minutes. Whisk the buttermilk dressing; 8 minutes. Dress the slaw and put it in the refrigerator for at least 45 minutes so the cabbage softens.

Grill
Light the kettle an hour before you eat; 25 minutes to a clean bed of coals. Grill the sausages for 14 minutes. Grill the corn for 10 minutes. Toast the buns for 3 minutes, last, so they stay warm.

Table
Set out plates, pickles and sauce once the buns are off; 10 minutes. Call everyone over when both cooks say it is ready; 5 minutes to lay it all out.
>>>

The recipe is a backyard barbecue for about twelve people: a pork shoulder smoked for roughly ten hours total, then held wrapped in a cooler for one to three hours and pulled, plus sausages, corn, buns, beans, and slaw prepared mainly in the final two hours and finished at the table. There is no stated deadline, so the schedule should finish as early as the work allows. The main constraints are single-instance equipment and timing: one offset smoker dedicated to the pork, one kettle grill for sausages/corn/buns, one side burner for the beans, one cooler for holding the shoulder, and only two cooks available. Several things have to hold, rest, or be ready at specific moments: the smoker must reach temperature before the shoulder goes on, the shoulder must be wrapped and returned to the smoker, the cooler hold is flexible, the beans and slaw start when the pork enters the cooler, and the kettle fire, sausages, corn, buns, and table set-out must be sequenced so the final grilling items finish in the right order.

A track is a single sequential line of work: steps within it run one after another and must not overlap, while truly concurrent activities belong on separate tracks. A step has exactly one duration type: fixed seconds, variable with min/max/default, or indefinite until the person ends it. A startTrigger anchors a step to either the program clock or to the completion/start of another step, including offsets, buffers, manual, abort, and compound choices. Step identifiers must be unique across the whole program, and each resource-consuming task named in a step needs a resourceConstraints entry whose maxConcurrent caps simultaneous use. Repeated batches should be modeled as one step with replicates, using instances each/all on downstream triggers, and maxInFlight when a holding area limits how many instances can be waiting at once.

- `offset_smoker`: `maxConcurrent: 1`, one physical smoker, shared across both cooks when they touch it  
- `kettle_grill`: `maxConcurrent: 1`, one kettle grill, used sequentially by either cook  
- `side_burner`: `maxConcurrent: 1`, one side burner for the beans  
- `cooler`: `maxConcurrent: 1`, one holding cooler for the wrapped shoulder  
- `refrigerator`: `maxConcurrent: 1`, one refrigerator for the slaw rest  
- `prep`: `maxConcurrent: 2`, both cooks can perform prep work at the same time  
- Overall staffing: two cooks
